The authors propose that Christian caregivers not only need to think about the p.sychological differences between shame and guilt, but should attend to resources from the Christian tradition that can help identify how shame and guilt differ. This article draws on the theology of St. Irenaeus to offer some theological reflections on differences between shame and guilt and reflects on the implications of these distinctions for care giving. The experience and effects of shame have been the focus of several recent boolis by Chris- tians (Capps, 1993; Fowler, 1996; Pattison, 2000; Smedes, 1993). These authors build on research in the psychology of shame that makes impor- tant theoretical and practical distinctions between shame and the closely related emotion of guilt (Erikson, 1963; Lewis, 1971; Tangney, 1995). These distinctions have implications for clinical understanding and response to individu- als experiencing shame and raise important questions. Should care for those experiencing shame be significantly different from care for those experiencing guilt? Despite the arguments of Capps (1993) and Fowler (1996) that shame, rather than guilt, is a more problematic emotion in Western culture, Christian caregivers have not developed theologies of shame that might bal- ance the current preoccupation with theologies of guilt (Capps, 1993; Pattison, 2000). This article presents a brief argument on the need for a the- ological understanding of shame and how shame differs from guilt. The authors seek to respond to this need by offering some theological reflections on the problem of shame inspired by the writing of Irenaeus, 2""J Century bishop of Gaul. The article concludes by considering implications of these theological reflections regarding how one cares for those experiencing shame. The Need for a Theological Understanding of Shame Shame and Guilt Are Different Emotions Shame and Guilt Are Often Confounded. Gilbert, Pehl, and Allan (1994) point out that Correspondence regarding this article should be addressed to Stephen Parker, Ph.D., Regent University, 1000 Regent University Drive, Virginia Beach, VA 23464. guilt and shame are often assumed to be inter- changeable or synonymous terms in Western cul- ture. Although a significant literature has developed on shame as a distinct clinical issue in the last few years (Dearing & Tangney, 2002; Nathanson, 1992; Tangney, 1995), Christian care- givers have not tended to take this shift into account, but continue to respond to shame as though it were no different than guilt (Capps, 1993; Fowler, 1996). This failure to distinguish adequately between shame and guilt has pro- duced confusing and ineffective care for those suffering from shame. Often such people are counseled toward confession and forgiveness, which are appropriate responses to guilt but pre- mature or ineffective responses to shame. Chris- tian caregivers need to take account of the clinical distinctions between shame and guilt and to offer theological reflections on the significant differences between these two emotions. Shame Is Neglected as a Significant Category for Theological Thought The confounding of shame and guilt in Chris- tian thought has contributed to the neglect of shame as a category for theological reflection. Pattison (2000) has pointed out the paucity of the church's theological reflections on the problem of shame, noting that the bulk of the Western Chris- tian tradition has focused on salvation as con- cerned with "guilt, offence, and forgiveness" (p. 190). Shame, even when noted, often is sub- sumed under the category of guilt. Theologian John Hick i\911') attributes the church's emphasis of guilt over shame to the extraordinary influence of Augustine. Hick particularly notes that the Augustinian interpretation of the creation story in the first three chapters of Genesis is one that emphasizes guilt. In the Augustinian reading of 176 THOMAS AND Parker 177 the text, one is drawn to see that perfect (better understood as mature) humans misused their God-given freedom, thus ushering evil into the world. Augustine emphasizes the autonomy (i.e., rebellious disobedience) of the primal couple. Because humans were created in a fully mature state, their willful disobedience requires punish- ment from a just God. This Augustinian "theology of the fall" (into sin) has tended to obscure the shame elements present in the text. One might even interpret the current preoccupation with forgiveness therapies and interventions as a sign of the continued emphasis of guilt over shame (cf. Enright & Fitzgibbons, 2000; McCullough, Sandage, & Worthington, 1997). The result is that shame goes "under-diagnosed" or misdiagnosed by pastors and clinicians. Shame, Not Guilt, Is the Dominant Cultural Emotion The early distinctions between "guilt" cultures in the West and "shame" cultures in the East (Benedict, 1946) reflected an overly simplistic (and biased) way to think about the differences between experiences of shame and guilt. Build- ing on a Freudian analysis of the neuroses, Bene- dict argued that guilt cultures were supposedly more advanced because they focused on individ- ual autonomy while shame cultures were more group focused. Such a position is no longer ten- able. Capps (1993) points to the work of Kohut (1971) and others to argue that shame, not guilt, is now the dominant debilitating emotion with which those in Western culture struggle. The shift from a concern with guilt to the impact of shame as a way to think about the human condition has important theoretical and practical implications (Thomas, 2002), yet Christian caregivers have only recently begun to recognize and reflect on this shift. As Capps (1993) notes No one has addressed in a systematic way the specific problem of how to reflect on sin within a cultural milieu in which shame, not guilt, is the pre- dominant experience, the more deeply felt emotion. Christian theolo- gy has well-developed theologies of guilt, while the majority of its con- stituency is struggling with the debili- tating, demoralizing, and even dehumanizing effects of shame, (p.3) The continued neglect of shame as a distinct category, either through subsuming it under guilt, or ignoring its importance altogether results in ineffective care for those experiencing shame. The need to respond in more caring and helpful ways to those experiencing debilitating shame requires that Christian caregivers not only take account of the clinical distinctions between shame and guilt but that they also develop a theological rationale for understanding and responding to these differing emotions. The next section of this article seeks to recover some of the theological resources of the Christian tradition for understand- ing shame as an emotion distinct from guilt. Theological Reflections on Shame According to Hick (1977), the triumph of guilt as a category for theological reflection in West- ern culture can be attributed to the influence of Augustine. The same narratives that Augustine used to establish the guilt of the primal couple also are the first Scripture passages to introduce the concept of shame. The development of a theological understanding of shame begins by revisiting the creation narratives in the early chapters of Genesis. The Message of Genesis Three What are the messages of the early chapters of Genesis? How is one to read these chapters as part of the salvation story? According to the Gene- sis texts, there is a time when Adam and Eve were naked and "not ashamed." After eating of the forbidden fruit, they have an awareness of their nakedness. This awareness causes them to hide. The implication is clear: they are experienc- ing a new emotion, that of being ashamed. Yet the shame elements of the story are generally overshadowed by interpretations that focus on the punishment meted out to the couple. This focus on their violation of the commandment not to eat of the forbidden tree gives a clear "guilt" cast to the story. To call attention to the shame elements in this story is not to deny that guilt elements are an important part of the understanding one should take from this story, nor is it to negate the important insights of Augustine on understanding this text. To call attention to the shame elements is simply to point to neglected dimensions of the story that can offer some insight into the nature of shame and how one might respond to it. An Alternate Emphasis: Irenaeus on Genesis Three As already noted, the dominance of a guilt reading owes much to Augustine's interpretation and the influence of that interpretation on the West. However, as Hick (1977) and others (e.g.. 178 TOWARD A THEOLOGICAL UNDERSTANDING OF SHAME Fowler, 1996) atso note, there are other theologi- cal voices that offer alternative insights into the significance of this story. One voice is that of Ire- naeus. His interpretation of these texts offers an understanding that opens one to see the shame elements noted there. Irenaeus of Lyons, who pre-dated Augustine by two centuries, is best known for his efforts to refute the teachings of Gnosticism in the 2"'' Century through his several volume work enti- tled Against the Heresies. These writings were directed toward contemporary Christians of that time, whose theological views he felt had run astray (Minns, 1994). While it could not be said that Irenaeus represented the whole of 2"'' Cen- tury Christianity, he did represent the majority views outside Alexandria, where Christian specu- lative thought was closer to the Gnosticism he fought (Grant, 1997). Genesis Three as a Story of Human "Development" In contrast to Augustine, who saw the world as a place of perfection before humankind's will- ful fall, Ireneaus believed that humankind was brought into an imperfect world by design. In the Irenaean view, the world was purposely imperfect, because it was designed to prompt the development of humankind spiritually (Fowler, 1975; Minns, 1994). He believed that the world exists as an environment for human life, and that imperfections are necessary and integral for the purpose of "soul-making" (Hick, 1977, p. 253). Ireneaus argues that while "it was possible for God Himself to have made man perfect from the first, ... man could not receive this [perfec- tion], being as yet an infant" (Against the Here- sies IV. xxxviii:l).i Thus, Irenaeus viewed the Genesis story as a metaphor of humankind's process of development in relationship to Par- ent-God over historical time, the themes of which are mirrored in the human developmental process from infancy to adulthood. Irenaeus argues that it is the nature of created beings always to grow and develop because they always are less than the Creator. In the Irenaean tradition, God accepts ultimate responsibility for the imperfect, necessarily developing humans, and the Irenaean perspec- tive seeks to show that there is good reason God created a universe in which evil was inevitable (Hick, 1977; Osborn, 2002). According to Ire- naeus, one of the reasons God creates in such a way that evil is present is that such a universe allows humans to be more "fully human" as they learn to discern between good and evil. "How, if he had no knowledge of the contrary, could he have had instruction in that which is good?....But if any one do shun the knowledge of both kinds of things [good and evil]...he unawares divests himself of the character of a human being" {Against the Heresies IV. xxxix:l). As Hick (1977) further observes: And so man, created as a personal being in the image of God, is only the raw material for a further and more difficult stage of God's creative work.... For personal life is essential- ly free and self-directing. It cannot be perfected by divine fiat, but only through the uncompelled responses and willing cooperation of human individuals in their actions and reac- tions in the world in which God has placed them. Men may eventually become the perfected persons who the New Testament calls 'children of God', but they cannot be created ready-made as this. (p. 254-255) This interpretation of the role of humans in God's creative activity emphasizes a different dimension than the Augustinian idea of original, but lost righteousness, and gives a clear "devel- opmental" cast to the Genesis narratives (Steen- berg, 2004). Reading the Genesis narratives as encapsulat- ing a developmental journey is suggestive regarding the role of shame as part of human development. Clearly, the developmental psy- chologist who has spoken most clearly on the developmental nature of shame is Erik Erikson (1963). Erikson's developmental model of the life crises suggests that shame is involved with the emergence of the self (his struggle of autonomy vs. shame and doubt) and is developmentally prior to guilt. Helen Block Lewis' (1971) seminal work on the differences between shame and guilt also highlights the idea that shame is more focused on the developing self while guilt is more the reflection of the developed self; The experience of shame is directly about the self, which is the focus of evaluation. In guilt, the self is not the central object of negative evaluation, but rather the thing done or undone is the focus. In guilt, the self is nega- tively evaluated in connection with THOMAS AND Parker 179 something but is not itself the focus of experience, (p. 30) One can see something of this more global neg- ative evaluation of the self in the remarks of the primal couple when confronted by God; "I was afraid because I was naked and I hid myself" (Genesis 3:10) focuses more on the self and its pain than on the acts committed (though those also are acknowledged afterwards—vs. 12,13). Reading the Genesis narratives as a story of human development also points to some phe- nomenological aspects of shame, such as the sense of exposure and vulnerability (i.e., being naked), and the resultant hiding and blaming behaviors (Genesis 3: 8-13; cf. Tangney, 1995). These phenomenological elements are sugges- tive in terms of care giving responses and are commented on below. Genesis Three as a Story of Broken Relationships In addition to the developmental focus, Ire- naeus places a clear focus on the relationships identified in these early chapters of Genesis. Part of God's creative purpose is that God's creatures would be in relationship to God and to one another. Irenaeus placed particular emphasis on the relationship between humankind and Cre- ator, believing most basically that humans were created for fellowship with God (Grant, 1997; Minns, 1994; Osborn, 2002). This, therefore, was the [object of the] long-suffering of God, that man, pass- ing through all things, and acquiring the knowledge of moral discipline, then attaining to the resurrection of the dead, and learning by experience what is the source of his deliverance ... might love Him the more..." (Against the Heresies III. xx.2). Clearly a central part of the story of Genesis 3 is that the previous fellowship with God is expe- rienced as broken. In hiding from God, the humans are experiencing an acute alienation from the One with whom they had walked and communed previously. Their confession of their nakedness is an anxiety ridden admission of the broken bond they are experiencing. That the previous relationship between the couple has suffered a rift is revealed in the blaming behav- ior, especially that of Adam (Genesis 3: 12). Understanding Genesis 3 as a story of broken relationships is not absent from the Augustinian interpretation of this story. However, Irenaeus' interpretation of this narrative emphasizes the broken relationships over the broken command- ments. It is the focus on broken relationships, not simply broken commandments, that helps one see the shame elements (in addition to the guilt elements) of the story. Though partaking of the forbidden fruit is a guilty act, the text clearly implies Adam and Eve also experienced shame. This experience of shame clearly indicates that the relationships with God and each other have changed. Interestingly, it is the nature of the bro- ken relationship that is actually the first element addressed by God. By asking, "Where are you?" God seeks first to re-establish contact with the hiding couple. The order of God's actions seem important. That is, the order of God's actions in the passage suggests that an appropriate response to guilt, which would include an effective means of remedy for one's misbehavior, takes place only when the underlying experience of shame is addressed through restoration of relationship. The overtly guilt-oriented reading of the Gene- sis text neglects those verses that focus on the shame experienced by the primordial couple and consequently overlooks God's action as address- ing their shame as well as their guilt. Thus, while guilt issues are clearly addressed in this text, this attention appears subsequent to addressing ele- ments of the primal couple's shame. This identification of developmental and rela- tional themes in the Genesis stories also helps identify important aspects of shame and its appropriate remediation. God (as Parent) addresses the shame and initiates and rebuilds a relational bridge (Kaufman, 1992). Humankind is thus empowered by Parent-God to maturely accept the consequences of their actions—they are enabled to experience appropriate guilt, hav- ing first had the underlying and overwhelming pain of their shame addressed. Thus, while Augustine primarily viewed the eviction from the Garden in terms of punishment for disobedience, the Irenaean tradition frames the sin of the primal couple as similar to the natural developmental process of children who must learn to choose good over evil as they move toward maturity. Irenaeus' commentary on the Genesis narra- tives gives a rather different emphasis than that of Augustine, and may sound strange to those deeply influenced by the latter. While Irenaeus' argument for the natural and necessary develop- ment of human beings was a key source in gen- erating the authors' theological reflections on 180 TOWARD A THEOLOGICAL UNDERSTANDING OE SHAME shame, one does not have to follow Irenaeus' theology in all its particulars (e.g., that the fall was intended by God), in order to appreciate how his perspectives on human/divine relation- ships and spiritual growth contribute to a theo- logical understanding of shame. The differences between shame and guilt noted in the Genesis narratives are important and share some common ground with recent psychological research on the distinctions between shame and guilt. First, the elements of shame are connected to a context of broken relationships while the guilt elements are connected to the broken command- ment. This distinction refiects Lewis' (1971; cf. Tangney, 1995) understanding that guilt concerns the thing done while shame involves a hiding and withdrawal from the Other. The phenomenologi- cal elements of shame, including feelings of expo- sure (nakedness), hiding, and blaming behaviors, are also manifestations of a breach in relation- ships. Shame-inspired behaviors (e.g., hiding, blaming) cause withdrawal from relationships; guilt-based behaviors (e.g., confession, accepting responsibility) move one toward reparation or restoration of relationship (Tangney, 1991). Second, shame, as distinguished from guilt, seems to involve a more global negative assess- ment of the self rather than involving a self that can distinguish itself from its bad actions. The primal couple's concern with their nakedness seems to involve more of the total self. "I was afraid because I was naked and I hid myself" seems a more global assessment of the self than "I ate." In the latter, the self appraises its actions, whereas the former statement is an appraisal of the self (by itselO. This difference can be seen, for instance, in the case of parents who engen- der a sense of shame in their children as a means of control. The child feels shame even when there was no "thing done" by the child. It is the child's self, not just the actions of the self that seems flawed to the child (and often to the adult who brings such lingering shame to coun- seling). Thus, shame seems to disrupt the emerg- ing self and its development, preventing the self from assessing and accepting its actions. God's actions in addressing the hiding self ("Where are you?") before addressing the self s actions seem to reflect this developmental sequence. Caregiving Implications of a Theological Understanding of Shame The Genesis narratives tell a story in which both shame and guilt elements are interwoven. This story refiects the fact that these two emo- tions often co-occur in people's lives, and thus are easily confused, both by those suffering from these emotions and by those who offer them care. The theological refiections on shame devel- oped here suggest some criteria for distinguish- ing whether people may be stniggling primarily with shame or guilt. It also suggests some differ- ences regarding how one might respond to those for whom shame is a predominant mani- festation. The implications for care giving include differences in treatment order, treatment focus, and treatment method. Treatment Order If one has determined that shame, rather than guilt, is the predominant emotion in a person's life, the theological refiections delineated here suggest that the shame should be addressed prior to addressing the guilt. These refiections on the treatment order grow out of the develop- mental emphasis in Ireneaus' interpretation of the Genesis narratives. The relationship between shame and guilt noted there is one in which God responded to the shame aspects exhibited by the primal couple before responding to their guilty acts. While clearly not a uniform conclusion, certain components of some clinical theories suggest a similar response (Erikson, 1963; Kohut, 1971; cf. Lewis, 1971). The idea that shame is develop- mentally prior to guilt is reminiscent of Erik Erik- son's (1963) progression of the life stages. That shame is the more developmentally primitive emotion is also arguable from Kohut's (1971) dis- tinctions between "guilty" humanity and "tragic" humanity. According to Kohut, the tragic client is much different than the guilty client of Freud's day. The guilty client had a stable personality that permitted the experiencing of guilt over the actions of the self, whereas the tragic client struggles with a more primitive and pervasive disturbance around the coherence of the self. The experience of shame shares this more per- vasive quality. Shame involves a more global condemnation of the self itself, rather than being able to make less global distinctions between the self and its condemnable actions. Often people are struggling with both shame and guilt. Because guilt is often easier to focus on (Capps, 1993; Fowler, 1996), the shame elements of a person's experience often are downplayed or ignored by caregivers. The theological refiections on shame offered here suggest that the opposite THOMAS AND Parker 181 ought to be the case for effective care giving. This shift in emphasis and order is important because when shame is the predominant feeling being experienced, it is the development of the self that needs attention, whereas when guilt is the pre- dominant emotion, it is the acts of the self that need attention. Effective care would mean that the sense of shame—the overwhelming sense that it is oneself who is bad, not just one's actions—needs to be addressed prior to working with the guilt the person is experiencing. Because shame and guilt often co-occur, and because it is not always easy to distinguish which is the most prominent emotion, this sug- gestion regarding treatment order is not always easily implemented. Often caregivers find them- selves moving back and forth between the two emotions in actual treatment. Treatment Focus If shame is to be the focus of treatment, rather than guilt, how is one to tell when this change in focus is needed? Furthermore, how is the care of those suffering from shame different from the care of those experiencing guilt? When shame and guilt co-occur, it is not always easy to distinguish when one emotion is predominant over the other. However, if it is obvious that a person's description of the prob- lem more prominently features a global, nega- tive assessment of the self rather than a negative assessment of his or her actions, the caregiver would suspect that shame, rather than guilt, is the dominant emotion. When hiding and blam- ing are prominent, one would have similar sus- picions. However, such prominence is not always obvious. As a practical means for distin- guishing when shame is dominant, the caregiver may be suspicious of times when the remedies for addressing guilt are not working. That is, sometimes those suffering from shame, or shame mixed with guilt, address the debilitating emotions they are feeling through overt actions of repentance (asking forgiveness from God or others). If guilt is the dominant emotion, such actions should bring some sense of release and quite often become the means for healing the breach in relationships. If shame is the domi- nant emotion, however, such actions seem to have little effect and the person is back the next day or week or month, confessing the same sin and experiencing the same sense of his or her badness. When the appropriate actions for guilt do not seem to be effective, there is a strong possibility that it is shame, rather than guilt, that the person is experiencing. Shame, as distin- guished from guilt, needs a different response to promote growth. In treating shame, the focus is on nurturing the emergence of the self. By strengthening the emergent self, one is able to move it develop- mentally toward the point where the self becomes secure enough to take responsibility for its actions. Until the self becomes stable enough to distinguish itself from its actions, the person will continue to confuse the two. In working with debilitating shame, care involves nurturing the self so that it is able to move away from the glob- al self-condemnations that prevent the self from a realistic assessment of its actions and appropriate responses. By contrast, the treatment of guilt makes wrong actions the focus of treatment. To focus on the actions of the self assumes a more developed self that is able to separate itself from its actions. A "guilty" self no longer makes global assessments of its badness, but can assess the results of its actions, and, because it is not over- whelmed by a pervasive sense of badness, can plan appropriate reparative actions. Treatment Method Since nurturing the emergent self is the focus in treating shame, the method must be relational, not simply behavioral. Instead of methods that focus on problems or solutions, the first movement in treating shame is to construct a "relational bridge" (Kaufman, 1992). This relational focus min"ors the Genesis account where God is described as restor- ing the relational breach by asking the primal cou- ple where they are. Only after reconnecting relationally (finding the hiding self) does God address the actions of the couple. Shame, by its nature, involves a moving away from relationship, a hiding. Prematurely trying to address guilt feel- ings rather than one's sense of shame may be a way for the self to continue hiding. Before those suffering from shame can truly embrace "setting things right" as guilt requires, issues that lie at the core of the self must be addressed. A sensitive clinician who moves to affirm and value the shamed self begins the first steps to strengthening that self. Then the self can come to reflect upon its deeds with a less global evaluation, whether nega- tion of the self or its opposite-inappropriate blam- ing of the other. Thus, one comes to see that helping others overcome debilitating shame requires the caregiver to build strong relational bonds with the shamed self of the sufferer. 182 TOWARD A THEOLOGICAL UNDERSTANDING OE ISHAME Concluding Summary We have argued that effective care for shame and guilt requires that these emotions be distin- guished from one another. The authors drew from the theology of Irenaeus to offer refiections on the developmental and relational nature of shame. Behavioral indicators of a predominance of shame over guilt include hiding and blaming and global self-condemnations. The article sug- gests that care in situations when shame is the dominant emotion, involves attending to shame prior to addressing guilt by strengthening the emerging self through establishing supportive relationships with the shamed self.
